20850-prince-prigio:
A queen who scorns fairies rules the court where Prince Prigio grows up. She swears fairies never lived, though the royal family's own history brims with them. Andrew Lang sets that comic clash at the heart of his fairy tale.

Prigio, too clever for his own good, gets gifts he never asked for. Magic caps, swords, and carpets tumble him into droll scrapes. Lang retold old tales for a living, and here he invents with glee. Prince Prigio stays among his best-loved tales, sly and swift, with a hero who must learn that brains alone cannot win a heart.
21381-stories-of-ohio:
William Dean Howells, Ohio's most famous novelist, wrote these stories in 1897 to give readers the history of his home state in outline. He opens with the Ice Folk and the Earth Folk, when glaciers pushed down from the north and covered much of the earth. Ohio's story runs from the ice to the Civil War generation.

Chapters follow Ohio as part of France, then English. The forty years' war for the West comes next, then the captivities of James Smith, Boone, and Kenton. The torture of Colonel Crawford and the state's wickedest deed get their due. Howells drew on Parkman, Henry Howe's collections, and Roosevelt's Winning of the West, and says his purpose of truth never failed.
21770-the-author-of-beltraffio:
A young American admirer keeps a letter of introduction in his pocket for three weeks in this Henry James tale of 1885. He is too shy to use it. The author he longs to meet is Mark Ambient, whose novel Beltraffio has caused a stir, even a scandal. James calls the book the most complete statement yet of the gospel of art.

The narrator has read Beltraffio five times and holds his visit back like a trump card. When the meeting comes, the great man's home life proves stranger than his fame. James studies the gap between the public artist and the private man. It is one of his sharp early tales of art, worship, and disillusion.
21859-historical-sketches-volume-i-of-3-:
Essays on Turks, Cicero, Apollonius, and the early Church fill this first volume of John Henry Newman's Historical Sketches, reprinted here in 1908. Newman gathers pieces written across his career, one of them first framed when he was still an Anglican controversialist. His dedication to Bishop Moriarty of Kerry explains the oddity with grace. He says he could not ask a Catholic bishop's formal leave, yet inscribes the book to him anyway.

The Turks are studied in their long relation to Europe. Cicero gets a portrait as orator and statesman. Apollonius of Tyana and primitive Christianity bring the volume into the early Church. Newman writes history as a man of faith and letters, with long, balanced sentences and deep learning worn lightly.
22631-an-account-of-timbuctoo-and-housa-:
An Account of Timbuctoo and Housa Territories in the Interior of Africa is a travel narrative of the western Sudan, drawn from the life of a Moroccan merchant and pilgrim. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Few Europeans had seen Timbuktu, and accounts from Muslim travelers carried rare weight.

The sample follows its subject at twenty-seven, leaving Tetuan with a caravan for Egypt on pilgrimage to Mecca and Medina. He returned to trade from his native town, then sailed for Hamburg to buy linens and goods his commerce needed. Only after such a life did his knowledge of the interior take shape. The account preserves routes, peoples, and markets of Hausaland and Timbuktu as a working trader knew them.
an-african-millionaire-episodes-in-the-l:
Grant Allen's An African Millionaire tells episodes in the life of the illustrious Colonel Clay. Colonel Clay is a master swindler whose quarry is Sir Charles Vandrift. Vandrift, a South African diamond millionaire, is robbed again and again. His secretary and brother-in-law narrates each defeat with rueful admiration.

The Episode of the Mexican Seer opens the campaign of disguise. Diamond links, a forged old master, and a Tyrolean episode follow in the contents. Clay changes face, voice, and trade faster than detectives can follow. Allen, a science writer turned novelist, makes crime a duel of wits. Each story asks how the trick was done this time. The book is a rogue's gallery in reverse: the criminal is the hero, and the millionaire the comic victim.
california-romantic-and-resourceful-a-pl:
John F. Davis wrote California Romantic and Resourceful as a plea for Pacific Coast history. Davis, a San Francisco lawyer, grew the book from two addresses. One marked Admission Day at Colton Hall in Monterey in 1908. The other spoke to the Commonwealth Club in 1913, with statistics revised to that year's end.

His argument is simple: Californians must collect, preserve, and spread their own records before they vanish. He praises new works on San Francisco's beginnings and a university fellowship in Pacific Coast history. The love story of Concha Argüello, the presidio girl who waited for her Russian lover, illustrates the romance he means. Illustrations show missions, Sutter's Mill, and old Monterey. Davis writes as a booster with a historian's conscience, urging pride to fund archives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-and-dio:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Bobbio treats both the abbey and the diocese suffragan to Genoa, coterminous with the civil district of Bobbio in the province of Pavia. Suppressed from 1803 to 1817 and annexed in turn to Alessandria and Casale, the diocese was re-established by Pius the Seventh in 1818.

Bobbio owes its origin to the monastery founded by the Irish saint Columban in 614, after Lombard invaders had swept northern Italy. Under Bishop Antonio Gianelli a congregation of Oblates of St. Alphonsus Liguori arose in 1839, hearing confessions in prisons and hospitals and spreading good literature, while the Gianelliane sisters served beside them. The entry joins diocesan history to the abbey's great missionary past.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ajaccio:
Ajaccio, Adjacensis, comprises the island of Corsica. Formerly a suffragan of Pisa, since the French Concordat it has been Aix's suffragan. History's first known bishop was Evander, who assisted at Rome's council in 313. Before the Revolution Corsica held five other dioceses. Accia had been vacant since 1563. Aleria's bishop resided at Corte, Sagone's at Calvi, and Mariana's at Bastia. Nebbio was the fifth.

Pius X, appointing Desanti bishop in 1906, reserved the right to redraw diocesan limits, by which Bastia might be restored. Legend says bishops banished from Africa in 484 built Ajaccio's primitive cathedral with their own hands. The present late-sixteenth-century cathedral owes its building to Gregory XIII, who as Ugo Buoncompagni had served at Ajaccio as papal legate. Greek-rite services continue at Cargese, founded in 1676 by descendants of Stephen Comnenus, expelled from the Peloponnesus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alessio:
Alessio, also called Lissus, is a diocese in European Turkey, suffragan of Scutari since 1886. It is one of the chief seaports of Albania, favourably placed near the mouth of the Drin. It once had five churches, and its cathedral, dedicated to St. Nicholas, once held the remains of the patriot George Castriota, known as Skanderbeg. On rocky hills across the Drin stand the church and convent of St. Anthony of Padua.

Within the diocese lies the quasi-episcopal abbey of St. Alexander of Orosci, an abbey exempt from any bishop's jurisdiction. The entry's sources include Farlati's Illyricum Sacrum, Gams's series of bishops, and Hecquard's Upper Albania, works that trace the diocese through centuries of change on Albania's coast.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexis-franco:
Alexis-François Rio was a French writer on art, born on the Island of Arz in Morbihan in May 1797 and dead in June 1874. Educated at Vannes, where he first taught, he went to Paris hoping for a chair of history and was disappointed. His championship of Greek liberty drew the government's notice, which named him censor of the press, and he refused the post.

A Foreign Ministry post under minister de La Ferronays let Rio become, in Montalembert's phrase, for Christian art what Winckelmann had been to ancient art. He spent 1830 to 1860 travelling in Italy, Germany, and England. At Munich he met the spokesmen of contemporary Catholicism and learned the aesthetic ideal from Schelling. His Christian Art, begun in 1835, failed in France though welcomed in Germany and Italy. After years among England's Pre-Raphaelites and fresh tours of Europe's galleries, he published his studies in four volumes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-see-o:
Vexio, in Sweden, covered Kronoberg and the hundreds of Ostra, Westra, Ostbo, and Westbo in Jonkoping. John Sigfrid, an Englishman from Northumbria and court bishop to King Olaf Tryggvasson, left Norway for Sweden in 1002 and worked six years in Westergotland. About 1008 he reached Vexio, preached with success to Varend's heathens, built a wooden church there, and stayed until his death about 1030.

In 1158 Adrian IV canonized him, and his shrine graced the Cathedral of Saint John the Baptist and Saint Sigfrid until the Reformation. He left no immediate successors, and in 1126 King Sigurd Jorsalafarer of Norway led a crusade into Smaaland to Christianize its people. Varend belonged to Skara until 1100, then to Linkoping, until Vexio was re-erected about 1150. Stenar, first bishop, appears in letters from 1183, quarrelled with Linkoping over frontiers in 1191. John Ehrengisleson followed in 1193. A life of Saint Sigfrid was written in 1205.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-del-ve:
Andrea del Verrocchio was born at Florence in 1435 and died at Venice in 1488. Born Andrea di Michele di Francesco de' Cioni, he took the name of his master, the goldsmith Giuliano Verrocchio. Some say he frequented Donatello's and Baldovinetti's studios, but goldsmith training marks his work, above all in delicate chasing, seen in the Colleoni horse and harness.

He excelled in children and womanly grace. He never married, living in his sister's household. Favoured by Lorenzo de' Medici, he was reputed the greatest artist of his time, yet seems never to have known fortune's favours, though his art shines with smiling beauty. Painter and sculptor, he worked as a sculptor: the Medici tomb at San Lorenzo and his bronze David at the Bargello. His Baptism of 1470 broke with the fresco school. Vasari called his manner hard and crude and claimed Leonardo painted the angel guarding Christ's garments.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-pallad:
Andrea Palladio, an Italian architect, was born at Vicenza in 1508 and died at Venice in 1580. Tradition makes him a poor carpenter's son, without a surname, until the poet Gian Giorgio Trissino, his patron, gave him the name Palladio, for Pallas, Greek goddess of wisdom. After a brief sculptor's apprenticeship he travelled, studying classical remains and seeking their principles with Vitruvius as guide.

His earliest known building is the Palazzo Godi at Lonedo, from 1540. Work on rebuilding his native town's basilica began in 1549, and its colonnades remain his most famous work. His triumphal arch at Vicenza still ranks as the best modern imitation of a Roman arch. Proportion, refinement, and invention mark his Vicenza palaces. He designed many villas, though few were finished. His writings spread his influence across Europe, with Inigo Jones as English editor, and American Georgian architecture descends from him. His manner is now called Palladian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-bosio:
Antonio Bosio, born in Malta about 1576 and dead in 1629, gave up law at eighteen to map the underground burial places of early Christians in Rome. A chance find on the Via Salaria in 1578 had stirred brief interest, yet almost no one pursued it further. Bosio made the work systematic, and the article credits him as the founder of Christian archaeology, the study of early Christian remains and sites.

He read widely before he dug, turning to acts of martyrs, council records, and Greek and Latin church fathers for clues to lost sites. That book learning guided his search through the catacombs, the tunnel burial grounds beneath Rome. Readers who want the birth of a field will find here a life spent joining texts to tunnels, so that scattered graves became a mapped record of the early church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arnolfo-di-ca:
Arnolfo di Cambio, sometimes called di Lapo, principal master of Italian Gothic, was born at Florence about 1232. He died there in his seventy-first year, probably in 1300, during Dante's brief power. Who Arnolfo was is scarcely known, though few architects left greater works. Baldinucci, Cicognara, and Gaye say his father Cambio came from Colle in the Val d'Elsa. Arnolfo first appears among workmen on the Siena cathedral pulpit as pupil or journeyman of Nicola Pisano.

With him worked a certain Lapo, called by Vasari his father, by others his instructor, but very likely only a fellow workman. The same band under Nicola worked at Pisa, Perugia, Cortona, Orvieto, and Rome. Arnolfo had reached thirty when his father died, already of high repute, having learnt from his father whatever that master knew. The entry follows a Gothic builder from workshop hand to master of Florence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartholomew-o:
Bartholomew of San Concordio was a canonist and man of letters, born near Pisa about 1260, who died at Pisa in 1347. He joined the Dominicans in 1277, studied at Pisa, Bologna, and Paris, and taught at Lucca, Florence, and Pisa. A renowned preacher, he matched learning with devotion and skill in Latin and Tuscan poetry with mastery of canon and civil law.

His fame rests on the Summa de Casibus Conscientiae, alphabetically arranged and called Pisana, Pisanella, or Bartholomaea. Clear, concise, and current with newer laws, it was hugely popular in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. Early printers in Germany, France, and Italy took it up, and Nicholas of Osimo added a supplement in 1444. His De documentis antiquorum, in Tuscan as Ammaestramenti degli antichi, became a Tuscan classic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedict-of-s:
Benedict of San Philadelphio, also called Benedict the Moor, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in Sicily in 1526 to enslaved parents from Ethiopia, he was freed by his parents' master for their faithful service. From youth he lived a devout life and joined a new group of hermits, men who pray apart from the world.

When the pope dissolved that group, Benedict entered the Franciscans, a mendicant order of friars. His virtues raised him to superior of a Palermo monastery, an unusual honour for a lay brother of African birth. The entry presents a humble friar whose holiness outshone the limits his age set for him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernardine-a-: Bernardine a Piconio, born Henri Bernardine de Picquigny in Picardy in 1633, died in Paris in 1709. He joined the Capuchins in 1649 and taught theology with distinction. His best-known work, a threefold exposition of St. Paul's letters, appeared at Paris in 1703 and in English in 1706, and stayed popular with Bible scholars, alongside his exposition of the Gospels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernardino-te:
Bernardino Telesio, an Italian philosopher who rebelled against Aristotle, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born of a noble family at Cosenza in 1508, he died there in 1588 after study at Milan, Rome, and Padua. At Padua he became a recognised leader of the anti-Aristotelians, thinkers who rejected the Greek master's method and system.

Back in the south, under the patronage of Paul IV, he founded an academy at Cosenza. His chief work, On the Nature of Things According to Their Own Principles, appeared in part at Rome in 1565 and in full at Naples in 1587. The entry presents a bold natural philosopher who urged study of nature itself over books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-besancon-veso:
Besançon, an archdiocese in eastern France, receives a full entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Its land matches the departments of Doubs and Haute-Saône plus the Belfort district, but few dioceses changed shape so often in the nineteenth century. Concordats, Swiss parishes, and the loss of Alsace-Lorraine in 1870 all redrew its map.

Archbishops fill the middle, from Granvelle, minister of Philip II who built the Besançon palace, to Grammont, who fought Jansenism and moved the university from Dôle. Luxeuil, St. Columbanus's monastery, anchors its early fame. The entry is a diocese reshaped by every border war around it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bisarchio: Bisarchio, a Sardinian diocese suffragan to Sassari, takes a short entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Its bishop lives at Ozieri, though early Christian history there is unknown. The first bishop named is Costantino Madrone about 1102, followed by Pietro in 1116. After moves to Giracle and Ardera, and union with Alghero in 1503, Pius VII restored the diocese in 1803.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-henry-of-s:
Blessed Henry of Segusio, usually called Hostiensis, was a thirteenth-century Italian canonist, profiled in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Born at Susa, he died at Lyons in 1271 after studying Roman and canon law at Bologna, where he taught and took his doctorate in both laws. Teaching at Paris and a stay in England followed, with a mission from Henry III to Innocent IV.

Provost of Antibes and papal chaplain, he rose to Sisteron in 1244, Embrun in 1250, and Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia in 1262. His Summa on the Decretals became the standard canon-law textbook of the age. The entry presents the greatest canonist of his century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-jacopo-de-:
Blessed Jacopo de Voragine, Archbishop of Genoa and medieval writer of saints' lives, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Viraggio near Genoa about 1230, he died in 1298 after joining the Dominicans in 1244. Fame as a preacher spread through Lombardy, and he taught Scripture and theology before becoming provincial of Lombardy in 1267.

Made Archbishop of Genoa in 1292, he worked to reconcile the city's warring Guelph and Ghibelline factions, with brief success in 1295, and held a synod on the relics of St. Syrus. His Golden Legend, a vast collection of saints' lives, made him the Middle Ages' most-read hagiographer. The entry presents a peacemaker and a storyteller.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brancaccio:
The Brancaccio, an ancient Neapolitan family, gave Naples its Brancacciana Library, state officials, and seven cardinals between the fourteenth and seventeenth centuries. Two branches survive today, those of Ruffano and Brancaccio, and France's Brancas descend from the same stock. Their cardinals span schism, councils, and embassies. The family also gave the state many fine servants over the years.

Landolfo, made cardinal in 1294, served Boniface VIII and Clement V and attended Vienne. Luigi, a learned canonist, became Archbishop of Taranto and cardinal in 1408. Nicolo backed antipopes Clement VII and Benedict XIII. Rinaldo and Tommaso attended Constance, Francesco Maria, cardinal in 1634, even debated whether chocolate breaks a fast, and Stefano, cardinal in 1681, served as nuncio at Florence and Venice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cassano-all-i:
Cassano all' Ionio is a diocese suffragan to Reggio, its city in Cosenza province in Calabria, set in a fertile hollow of a steep mountain. Known in Caesar's time as Cassanum, its see has no known founding date, though a bishop appears in 1059 and another, Saxo, in 1096. Its bishops form a long roll. Antonello dei Gesualdi was learned in canon and civil law, and Belforte Spinelli attended Constance as a layman before retiring to Venice.

Later names include Cristoforo Giacoazzi, called to Rome by Paul III for his skill in church affairs, and Giovanni Angelo Medici, afterwards Pius IV. An Englishman, Audoeno Ludovico Cambrone, sent on papal missions, never lived in Cassano. Theatines and Augustinians follow in the list, and the diocese counts 130,000 people in 46 parishes, with 200 churches and chapels and 263 priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-comacchio:
Umberto Benigni's entry covers Comacchio, a diocese suffragan of Ravenna. The town lies in Ferrara province in the Romagna, on islands near the mouths of the Po. A canal built by Cardinal Palotta joins it to the sea. Its old name was Cymaclum. Pacatianus, present at a Roman synod in 503 under Pope Symmachus, stands as its first known bishop. Saint Gregory the Great counts the see among Ravenna's suffragans. In the fifteenth century Venice held the town, but Alfonso II of Ferrara retook it in 1509.

At Alfonso's death in 1597, Comacchio passed with Ferrara under the Holy See. Bishop Alfonso Pandolfo, in 1631, wrote polished verse and prose and founded the Accademia dei Fluttuanti. Nearby stands the shrine of Santa Maria in Aula Regia, reached by a portico of 142 arches from 1647. The diocese counted 40,630 people, with 114 parishes, 26 secular and 6 regular priests, and the famed Benedictine Abbey of Pomposa within its bounds.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SecondGrandJury:
Donald P. Baker reported for the Washington Post on July 20, 1973, that a second federal grand jury had been authorized in the Watergate matter. This jury would investigate campaign finances: campaign corruption and illegal corporate contributions. The first jury had handled the break-in itself. The second would follow the money.

govdocs-archive_org-the-advisory-committ:
President Clinton created the Advisory Committee on Human Radiation Experiments to face a buried scandal. Its final report, issued in October 1995, examines Cold War tests in which the government exposed citizens to radiation, often without their knowledge or consent.

Committee staff read secret files and heard from victims and officials. The report names the experiments, judges them by the ethics of their own time and ours, and asks what the government owes the people it used. It stands as a landmark of bioethics, and as proof that official secrecy can be opened by patient public work.
govdocs-archive_org-ufos-fact-or-fiction:
Gregory W. Pedlow and Donald E. Welzenbach wrote the CIA's own history of its spy planes. The Central Intelligence Agency and Overhead Reconnaissance covers the U-2 and OXCART programs from 1954 to 1974.

The U-2 photographed the Soviet Union from extreme altitude until one was shot down in 1960. OXCART, the A-12, flew even faster and higher. As the agency's official history, the book explains budgets, bases, cameras, and politics from inside records. It became a landmark of intelligence history, not least because many UFO reports of the era traced back to these secret flights.
henry-ossian-flipper-the-colored-cadet-a:
Henry Ossian Flipper wrote his autobiography as the first man of color to graduate from the United States Military Academy at West Point. Flipper, born enslaved in Georgia, won an appointment to the academy and endured four years in which white cadets largely refused to speak to him. His book tells that ordeal plainly: the silence, the inspections, the loneliness, and the discipline of a cadet who could not afford one failure.

He graduated in 1877 and took a lieutenant's commission in the cavalry. The memoir is a young officer's account of proving himself inside an institution that doubted his right to be there. It stays a key firsthand document of race and the American army after the Civil War.
klondyke-nuggets-a-brief-description-of-:
Joseph Ladue wrote Klondyke Nuggets in September 1897, at the height of the gold rush. Ladue was an explorer, miner, and prospector. He also founded Dawson City in the Northwest Territories.

Ladue wrote because crowds of people kept asking him for facts. His short book describes the gold regions of the Northwest Territories and Alaska. He promised a larger book with maps, pictures, and practical details for newcomers. Prospectors planning the hard trip north could start with his firsthand account. He stresses facts over rumor, which gold rush readers badly needed. His brief guide also preserves the mood of that frantic season.
nasa-tm-19650025654-limits-on-collisionl:
C M Goldstein at Lewis Research Center examined the limits of a simple model for thermionic converters in this journal article draft. Such a converter turns heat directly into electric power. Its heart is a diode filled with gas, across which current flows. The simple model assumes the particles inside never collide with each other.

Goldstein asks where that collisionless picture breaks down. Current against voltage curves for gaseous diodes frame the test. A model that fails silently can mislead a power system design. Space power systems were a likely user of such converters. Knowing a model's limits is as useful as the model itself.
nasa-tm-19670003836-some-observations-on:
J. S. Theon, W. Nordberg, and L. B. Katchen, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this October 1966 paper with J. J. Horvath of the University of Michigan. It reports temperature and wind observations in the mesosphere, the cold middle layer of the upper atmosphere, gathered by rocket soundings.

The soundings belonged to a Goddard program running since 1960. Launches came from sites in Alaska, Canada, and Virginia, plus Ascension Island and ships in the South Pacific. This paper presents newer 1964 and 1965 flights aimed at specific questions. They targeted the temperature structure inside shimmering noctilucent clouds and sudden stratospheric warmings with their circulation changes. Other flights probed wavy temperature patterns linked to gravity waves, and daily temperature swings near the stratopause predicted by tidal theory.
nasa-tm-19670020700-a-10-cps-periodicity:
David S. Evans wrote this paper at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in May 1967. It reports a rhythm in the aurora: a ten cycles per second pulsing in the rain of electrons into the auroral zone. Rocket-borne radiation detectors caught the pattern, which was purely a change in time, not a movement across the sky.

The pulsing appeared in electrons from low to fairly high energies, and the higher energy electrons fluctuated the most. Peaks at two very different energies arrived with no measurable time shift between them. That timing places the mechanism causing the modulation within about a thousand kilometers of Earth. A strong beam of electrons at one steady energy was present at the same time. Evans proposes a process like runaway electron production in laboratory plasmas, where a growing plasma wave resonantly speeds favored electrons to high energy.
nasa-tm-19670029742-facilities-for-simul:
Herbert H. Hoop, of the Redstone Scientific Information Center in Alabama, surveyed test facilities in this report, dated June 30, 1967. The facilities simulate the attitude motion of spacecraft. They use gas bearings, which float a platform on a cushion of gas so it can rotate almost without friction.

The survey was requested by the Guidance and Control Division at Marshall Space Flight Center. Hoop describes facilities at twelve government and industrial organizations. Typical entries cover the test chamber, bearing, platform, and power needs. They also cover balance, test procedures, sensors, and how data gets out. Builders of attitude control systems could find a rig that fit.
nasa-tm-19680010575-automatic-pressure-t:
Albert E. Schuler, at the Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama, describes a labor-saving rig in this memorandum. The rig calibrates pressure transducers automatically. Transducers turn pressure into electrical signals, and their readings drift, so they must be checked often.

Schuler traces how the work evolved from past practice. Older systems gave way step by step to an automatic one. The new system handles the calibration itself and passes the data to a computer. The report covers that development in detail. Such rigs kept the flood of test sensors at a big center honest and traceable.
nasa-tm-19680012931-a-spacecraft-analog-:
Sensor readings aboard a spacecraft start as smooth voltages, but computers need numbers. This report describes an analog-to-digital conversion system built for spacecraft to bridge that gap. Its parts include an analog commutator and a gated voltage-to-frequency converter, with the digital output stored.

The contents trace the converter's development history and its system requirements. A section explains the MOSFET device itself, then the commutator, oscillator, and voltage regulator. The digital accumulator and the oscillator's measured performance follow. The abstract stresses the system's very high input impedances and compactness. Those traits suit it to many uses beyond one spacecraft.
nasa-tm-19680015819-a-use-of-lighthill-s:
Ernest S. Armstrong of NASA's Langley Research Center applies Lighthill's generalized functions to optimal control problems in this paper, presented in May 1967. Optimal control asks how to steer a system in the best possible way. Its two-point boundary value problems can be hard to solve with standard tools.

Armstrong first explains generalized functions in plain terms. The famous delta function seems to break normal math rules, since it vanishes everywhere except one point. Thinkers such as Schwartz and Halperin built rigorous ways to handle such objects. Armstrong then uses Lighthill's approach to work through control problems. The paper gives engineers a cleaner mathematical path to those solutions.
nasa-tm-19690016023-on-the-numerical-sta:
D. Sugimoto wrote this Goddard preprint, numbered X-641-69-138, on whether star life computations stay numerically stable. Computer models follow a star's life shell by shell, balancing gravity's squeeze against heat flow. Sugimoto studies a serious instability that grows from coupling those two processes together in the arithmetic.

A heat wave may or may not cross into the next shell within one time step, he explains. Slow and rapid evolution demand different physical pictures, and core and envelope differ greatly in how fast heat flows. Choosing the wrong picture breeds the instability. After probing its nature, Sugimoto shows one math scheme can serve both cases. It fits the picture that rapid or slow evolution requires, in core or envelope alike.
nasa-tm-19690025296-propulsion-systems-f:
W. E. Moeckel of Lewis Research Center asks what propulsion can make interplanetary travel fast in this August 1969 memorandum. Only a few systems promise trip times comparable to sixteenth-century terrestrial expeditions, he notes. The report links planetary round-trip times to propulsion performance parameters.

Two system types frame the analysis. Type I is specific-impulse limited with high thrust, while Type II is specific-mass limited with low thrust. Moeckel discusses advanced concepts of both types and evaluates their limits. Concepts include solid, liquid, and gaseous core fission rockets, plus nuclear-pulse and nuclear-electric systems. Thermonuclear fusion rockets get particular attention, being less familiar than the others.
nasa-tm-19700001371-turbulence-from-the-:
J. R. Herring wrote this October 1969 preprint, numbered X-641-69-441, on turbulence from the distribution function point of view. Statistical theory describes a turbulent flow by the odds of finding each possible velocity pattern. Herring describes and compares two recent approaches built on that idea, one by Edwards and one from his own earlier work.

Both expand the flow's probability distribution around its single-point form, he explains. They differ, at second order, only in how swirling relaxation rates are set. Herring tests their energy spectrum predictions against exact numerical results for simple systems. He closes on a shared flaw: neither yields the proper Kolmogorov inertial range spectrum, and he suggests a fix.
nasa-tm-19700008822-multigroup-resonance:
Gerald P. Lahti and Robert M. Westfall of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in January 1970. It gives nuclear cross sections for tungsten and for depleted uranium. Cross sections state how likely atoms are to catch or scatter passing neutrons.

The pair calculated the values for the resonance region, where neutron capture changes sharply with energy. The values cover slabs of each metal and are grouped by energy band. They were made for use in shielding calculations. Designers of nuclear space power systems used such tables to size shields that keep radiation away from crews and gear.
nasa-tm-19710013891-thermally-stable-pol:
T T Serafini, P Delvigs, and G R Lightsey of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for an April 1971 composites meeting in St Louis. It describes a way to make heat proof polyimide resins from simple liquid starting chemicals. Polyimides serve in fiber composites that must survive high heat. Older resin solutions were hard to store and work with.

Their method soaks graphite fibers in a solution of basic building blocks. Parts made from these soaked fibers kept their strength well at six hundred degrees Fahrenheit. They also resisted damage from hot air. The liquid kept a long shelf life and dissolved more easily. Both traits beat the older approach.
nasa-tm-19720013633-high-energy-astronom:
Program Development staff at the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this phase A final report in January 1972, as NASA TM X-64652. Volume two runs to more than seven hundred pages. It covers the High Energy Astronomy Observatory, mission C, in early design. HEAO would carry instruments for X-ray astronomy in Earth orbit. Phase A work tests whether a mission concept is sound and affordable.

The volume presents a baseline mission and spacecraft design. It starts with the planned X-ray experiments themselves. Mission needs are analyzed next, followed by the observatory design. Structural analysis, heat control, and attitude control all receive treatment. Such a volume fixed the design before hardware money flowed.
nasa-tm-19720015848-apollo-14-composite-:
I G Yates Jr of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this final report in October 1971, as NASA TM X-64641. Yates worked in the Process Engineering Laboratory. The subject is a casting experiment flown on Apollo 14. On Earth, mixed materials of different weights separate as they melt and freeze. The demonstration asked whether low gravity would keep them blended. A positive answer would open new ways to make composite materials.

Astronauts ran the experiment during the quiet coast phases of the flight. Sealed metal capsules held low melting model materials and dispersing agents. An electric heater melted each charge, and a heat sink cooled it. The crew processed the full set of samples aloft. Evaluation compared the space cast samples with ground controls.
of-genius-in-the-occasional-paper-and-pr:
Two short Augustan texts are reprinted together here. One is the anonymous essay Of Genius from 1719. It appeared in The Occasional Paper, volume three. The other is Aaron Hill's preface to The Creation from 1720. Gretchen Graf Pahl wrote the introduction to this reprint.

The reprint came out in 1949 in Los Angeles. It belongs to the Augustan Reprint Society series. The texts ask what genius is and how poets create. Hill defends his long religious poem in his preface. Together they show early debate about talent and taste. Scholars of Augustan literature still cite both short pieces today.
on-a-dynamical-top-for-exhibiting-the-ph:
James Clerk Maxwell read this paper in April 1857. It appeared in the Transactions of the Royal Society of Edinburgh. Maxwell studies a spinning top built with fine adjustments. He calls the common top a symbol of hard science. Great mathematicians had labored over its motion before him.

Euler, Lagrange, and others set the laws of rotation. Maxwell's top shows far more complex motions than earlier models. A colored disc makes the axis motion visible. He links the top to Earth's motion and precession. The paper blends deep mathematics with a working instrument. It shows Maxwell's gift for clear physical thinking.
on-the-trail-of-pontiac-or-the-pioneer-b:
Edward Stratemeyer wrote this frontier tale for young readers. It is volume four of his Colonial Series. Earlier volumes followed Dave Morris with young George Washington. Dave served in the Braddock expedition against Fort Duquesne. Later volumes treated Niagara and the fall of Montreal.

This tale turns to Pontiac and the Ohio frontier. Dave and his cousin Henry again do their duty well. Settler cabins and wilderness danger fill the adventure. Stratemeyer blends real campaigns with invented boy heroes. The book delivers history-flavored excitement at full gallop. A front picture shows the dance of the magicians. Its note says the dance lasted a full quarter hour.
podcast-joerogan-Xq2aJpDHIio:
Physician Zach Bush joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2529. Bush is a doctor who moved from standard practice toward soil, food, and the gut as the roots of health. His talks link farming chemicals to the chronic disease filling his clinics.

He tells Rogan how his view changed, from prescribing for symptoms to studying the microbiome and the land that feeds it. Rogan asks what a patient should do with advice that starts in a field. The episode is a wide, hopeful talk on health and nature, from a doctor who argues the two were never separate.
poems-of-nature-poems-subjective-and-rem:
John Greenleaf Whittier's works fill seven volumes, and this second volume gathers three great groups of his shorter poems: poems of nature, poems subjective and reminiscent, and religious poems. The nature section is a New England calendar in verse, from the Frost Spirit and Hampton Beach through April, the Mayflowers, and the Last Walk in Autumn. Whittier farmed the Merrimac valley country he sang, and local places crowd the contents.

Mountain pictures of Franconia and Monadnock, a storm on Lake Asquam, and the trailing arbutus show his range beyond the farm. The reminiscent poems turn inward to memory and friendship, while the religious poems carry the plain faith of a Quaker abolitionist. Readers who know Whittier only for Barbara Frietchie or Snow-Bound will find here the quieter poet his neighbors loved: a singer of one region's seasons, written into permanence.
radio-boys-cronies-or-bill-brown-s-radio:
Radio Boys Cronies, or Bill Brown's Radio, by Wayne Whipple and S. F. Aaron, is a boys' novel of the first radio years. Chapter one, The Cronies, hurries two friends across the town of Fairview to hear a program that Mr. Gray has promised will begin promptly at three.

Bill Brown, undersized, dark, and quick, gets about on a crutch because of a twisted knee, while his chum Gus Grier, big, fair, and athletic, is built like the opposite. When Bill lags, Gus hoists him onto his broad back and carries him a quarter of a mile, drawing shouts from the street-corner boys as they go.
sant-ilario:
F. Marion Crawford wrote Sant' Ilario, which he dedicated to his wife as the follow-up volume to Saracinesca. The opening chapter returns to Anastase Gouache, a painter readers met earlier. Two years of army service with the Zouaves have reshaped both his look and his habits.

Gouache remains slight, but sun and hard daily work have toughened him. His hair is cut short, his manner is watchful and quick, and the dreamy air he once had while painting portraits is gone. He still paints in his free hours in the studio. Looking back, he marvels that a circle around Donna Tullia Mayer once drew him into loose talk of plots and politics.
scotus-de-primo-principio:
John Duns Scotus wrote De Primo Principio, On the First Principle, in the early 1300s, and it appears here in the 1891 Vives edition of his works. Scotus, the Franciscan master known as the Subtle Doctor, taught at Oxford and Paris. The short treatise holds his proof of God's existence, the most rigorous of the Middle Ages.

Scotus argues step by step that an infinite regress of causes is impossible, so a first principle must exist, infinite and uncaused. The companion piece, the Theoremata, gathers brief propositions in the same exacting style. Every term is defined before it is used, and every step is challenged and defended. The proof became the high-water mark of scholastic argument. The Vives edition, a reprint of Wadding's seventeenth-century collection, kept this text before scholars of the modern age.
shakespeare-s-first-folio:
Early printed texts of Shakespeare's plays keep their old spelling in this copy of the First Folio, as an editor's opening notes explain at length. Hamlet's first lines stand as proof: Barnardo asks who's there, and the answer comes in old forms that look like errors to modern eyes.

The notes blame the printers' craft, not the poet: type was costly, sorts ran short, and letters such as u and v traded places. Scholars, the editor warns, prize these quirks highly. Readers meet the plays close to their first printed state, spelling, odd letters, and all.
the-adventures-of-pinocchio:
C. Collodi, pen name of Carlo Lorenzini, wrote The Adventures of Pinocchio, rendered from the Italian by Carol Della Chiesa. Chapter one tells how Mastro Cherry, a carpenter, found a piece of wood that wept and laughed like a child.

The narrator teases young readers who guess the tale starts with a king: it starts, he says, with a plain block of firewood. One fine day that log lands in the shop of old Mastro Antonio, called Mastro Cherry for his round, red, shiny nose. Readers follow the puppet carved from that wood through tricks, hunger, and hard lessons, in the famed Italian tale of a wooden boy who longs to be real.
the-author-of-beltraffio:
Henry James published the title tale in a Macmillan edition dated 1922 in London. A young American narrator tells how he kept a letter of introduction for three weeks before daring to visit Mark Ambient. He had read Ambient's novel Beltraffio five times and feared troubling a famed and irritable writer.

For the narrator, that book stood as a bold statement of art for its own sake. He recalls the stir, even scandal, it caused in England three years earlier. His visit becomes a study of awe, youth, and the gap between a reader who worships a book and the living author who wrote it.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-01-genesis-t: Front matter for a Douay-Rheims Bible names its two parts. The Old Testament was first printed at Douay in 1609 and 1610. The New Testament was printed at Rheims in 1582. Bishop Richard Challoner revised both in 1749 to 1752. A history tells how English exiles founded a college at Douay in 1568 under William Allen. Gregory Martin began an English translation for Catholic readers in 1578, helped by Allen, Richard Bristow, Thomas Worthington, and William Reynolds. No Genesis text itself appears in these pages.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-04-numbers-t:
Numbers, in a Douay-Rheims rendering from the Latin Vulgate, in Bishop Richard Challoner's revision of 1749 to 1752. Its New Testament line goes back to Rheims in 1582, its Old Testament line to Douay in 1609 and 1610. An introduction frames it as a history of almost thirty-nine years, reaching the eleventh month of the fortieth year.

Chapter one is set in the desert of Sinai, in the second year after the leaving of Egypt. God tells Moses to number the children of Israel. A heading adds that the Levites are set apart to serve the tabernacle rather than be counted with the others. Counting, ordering, and assigning service give the book its name and its opening action.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-09-1-kings-t:
First Kings in the Douay naming, in Douay-Rheims wording taken from the Latin Vulgate, with Bishop Richard Challoner's revisions of 1749 to 1752 applied. The New Testament portion traces to Rheims, 1582; the Old Testament portion to Douay, 1609 and 1610. An introduction reports a common view that Samuel wrote the book up to chapter twenty-five. Prophets Nathan and Gad, it says, finished the first book and wrote the second.

Chapter one tells of Anna, wife of Elcana, who was barren. By vow and prayer she obtains a son, names him Samuel, and presents him for God's service in Silo as she promised. The setting is Ramathaimsophim on Mount Ephraim. A child's birth, answered prayer, and a mother keeping a hard vow open a history of prophets and kings.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-10-2-kings-t:
Second Kings in the Douay naming follows David after Saul's death, in the version of Douay-Rheims, an English rendering of the Latin Vulgate revised by Bishop Richard Challoner over 1749 to 1752. Its two parts first appeared at Rheims in 1582 and at Douay in 1609 and 1610. David returns from the slaughter of the Amalecites and stays two days in Siceleg.

On the third day a man comes from Saul's camp with torn garments and dust on his head. He falls before David in reverence, bringing news from a lost battle. Mourning, report, and a new reign meet in a single scene. A kingdom changed by death is the book's tone from the start, and David is left to answer what the messenger claims.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-11-3-kings-t:
Third Kings in the Douay naming, in Douay-Rheims English drawn from the Latin Vulgate, in the revision Bishop Richard Challoner finished across 1749 to 1752. Rheims in 1582 supplied the New Testament, Douay in 1609 and 1610 the Old Testament. An introduction suggests the books were written by prophets of Israel who recorded, by inspiration, the chief events of their days.

Chapter one shows King David grown old, with Abisag a Sunamitess brought to him. Adonias claims the throne, but Nathan and Bethsabee act so that Solomon is declared and anointed king instead. Succession, court plotting, and a prophet's intervention fill the start. Readers see an ageing king, a rival son, and a mother securing the promised heir.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-12-4-kings-t:
Fourth Kings in the Douay naming opens with a sick king sending messengers, in a form of Douay-Rheims translated from Latin Vulgate wording and revised by Bishop Richard Challoner, 1749 to 1752. Behind the wording stand printings at Douay in 1609 and 1610 and at Rheims in 1582. They ask whether he will recover from his illness.

An angel sends Elias the Thesbite to meet those messengers with a sharp question: is there no God in Israel, that they go to consult Beelzebub? False gods, a prophet's rebuke, and a king's sickness collide at once. The scene sets a pattern for the book, in which prophets confront rulers who seek help outside the God of Israel. Elias speaks before any court scene unfolds.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-38-micheas-t:
Micheas, in Douay-Rheims English drawn from the Latin Vulgate, in the revision Bishop Richard Challoner finished across 1749 to 1752. Rheims in 1582 supplied the New Testament, Douay in 1609 and 1610 the Old Testament. An introduction warns that Samaria will be destroyed by the Assyrians, who will also invade Juda and Jerusalem.

Chapter one dates his word to the reigns of Joathan, Achaz, and Ezechias, kings of Juda. He is called the Morasthite, and his vision concerns Samaria and Jerusalem together. Two capitals under one judgment frame the book. A small-town prophet speaks to cities and rulers, joining blame for wrongdoing with a later promise that this edition's readers will find in his closing chapters.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-40-habacuc-t:
Habacuc, in a form of Douay-Rheims translated from Latin Vulgate wording and revised by Bishop Richard Challoner, 1749 to 1752. Behind the wording stand printings at Douay in 1609 and 1610 and at Rheims in 1582. Chapter one calls his message a burden that the prophet saw. A note explains that prophecies threatening grievous evils and punishments are especially called burdens.

An introduction fragment links his words to vengeance God will take by means of the Chaldeans. Questioning, rather than calm certainty, marks this short book: a prophet asks why wrong seems to win. The opening label alone prepares readers for complaint, a divine answer, and a final act of trust under threat.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-47-matthew-t:
Matthew, in a Douay-Rheims rendering from the Latin Vulgate, in Bishop Richard Challoner's revision of 1749 to 1752. Its New Testament line goes back to Rheims in 1582, its Old Testament line to Douay in 1609 and 1610. An introduction says his Gospel was translated into Greek in the apostles' time and was written about six years after the Ascension.

Chapter one is headed as the genealogy of Christ, conceived and born of a virgin. It opens as the book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham. Lineage comes before teaching or miracles. A Jewish family line, a virgin birth, and names linking Jesus to kings and patriarchs set the terms for the life that follows.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-65-hebrews-t:
Hebrews, in Douay-Rheims English, translated out of the Latin Vulgate and later revised by Bishop Richard Challoner (1749-1752). The Old Testament first came from Douay, in 1609 and 1610; the New Testament from Rheims, in 1582. An introduction places it in Italy, probably Rome, about twenty-nine years after the Ascension. It urges patience, perseverance, and brotherly charity.

Chapter one sets a contrast: God spoke of old by the prophets, but now by his Son. That Son, it says, is incomparably greater than the angels. No author is named in the letter's own opening here. Argument from scripture, warning against drifting, and praise of Christ's priesthood give this epistle its distinct, solemn voice.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-67-1-peter-t:
First Peter, in Douay-Rheims form, drawn from the Latin Vulgate and carried through Bishop Richard Challoner's revision, dated 1749 to 1752. An Old Testament printed at Douay in 1609 and 1610 and a New Testament printed at Rheims in 1582 lie behind the text. An introduction says Peter wrote at Rome, which he figuratively calls Babylon, about fifteen years after the Ascension. It stresses the authority given him by Christ.

Chapter one gives thanks for being called to true faith and eternal life, entered through many trials. Peter urges holiness of life, citing God's holiness and redemption by Christ's blood. Scattered believers under pressure are the letter's audience. Hope under suffering, rather than escape from it, is Peter's opening counsel.
the-english-governess-at-the-siamese-cou:
Anna Harriette Leonowens's The English Governess at the Siamese Court gives her account of six years in the royal palace at Bangkok. Her front pages carry a warm note to Mrs. Katherine S. Cobb, who urged her to try America rather than return to Siam, and who pled for her children. Pictures from photos given by the King of Siam are promised.

Leonowens taught the king's wives and children English and science. Her tale of court rites, harems, and slavery in Siam gripped Western readers. Later stage and film fame grew from her books.
the-satyricon-volume-02-dinner-of-trimal:
Volume two of W. C. Firebaugh's unexpurgated Satyricon translation is titled The Dinner of Trimalchio. It continues Petronius Arbiter's narrative at chapter the twenty-seventh. A bracket code marks passages by different hands. Parentheses signal forgeries of Nodot. Square brackets mark Marchena, and braces mark additions of De Salas.

The narrator and his companions stroll toward a circle of ball players. A bald old man in a russet tunic plays ball with long-haired boys. A slave stands by with a bag of balls, so none are retrieved. Two eunuchs attend, one holding a silver chamber-pot. Menelaus explains that this is their host. What they see, he pants, is only a prelude to the dinner.
the-wearing-of-the-green-or-the-prosecut:
A Dublin pamphlet of 1868 from A. M. Sullivan of Abbey Street takes its title from the song The Wearing of the Green. Its subject is a prosecuted funeral procession, and a poem from the Nation supplies the epigraph about tears flowing in silence while watch is kept on the foe. The narrative opens with the Manchester executions.

News of the hangings on Saturday, November 23, 1867, fell on Ireland with sudden, dismal disillusion. The three condemned men had lain weeks under sentence, yet nobody truly believed England would take their lives on a verdict already proclaimed a blunder. The pamphlet says the public conscience revolted, producing an upheaval of national emotion unseen in Ireland for a century.
twilight-and-dawn-or-simple-talks-on-the: Caroline Pridham, writing as Mrs. L. G. Wait, presents Twilight and Dawn as simple talks on the six days of creation. The contents begin with God's Book and an opening talk called In the Beginning. The days then unfold in order: light, the ocean of air, waters and the green earth, and the sun, moon, and stars. A story of a deaf boy sits inside the fourth day. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the talks themselves do not appear.
what-philately-teaches-a-lecture-deliver:
John N. Luff gave What Philately Teaches as a lecture in Brooklyn on February 24, 1899. The talk came out in a third edition in New York in 1915. Luff says he wrote for people who do not collect stamps. Old hands, he warns, will find much of it plain and known.

Stamp study, Luff argues, has grown past a child's hobby. It teaches facts and gives grown minds rest at once. He jokes that stamp albums should bear a Latin motto meaning thou teachest. A Chinese tea chest pun on the phrase makes his point with a laugh. Readers learn how small printed squares can teach lands, past events, and art.
